summary.text: Lucas’s theorem in base three and the evenness of central binomial coefficients give entry congruences making column \(j\) congruent to \((-1)^j\) times column zero modulo \(3\), and to column zero modulo \(4\); subtracting these multiples factors \(3^n\) and \(4^n\) from the determinant, while the \(n=1\) case upgrades the latter to \(16\mid a_n\) for every \(n\ge1\). Writing \(u=A(x/3)-1\) and expanding \((1+u)^{1/8}\), the coefficient of degree \(m\) in \(u^d\) inherits factors \(3^m\) and \(16^d\), which respectively cancel the scaling at \(p=3\) and the bound \(\lvert\binom{1/8}{d}\rvert_2\le16^d\); at every other prime the binomial coefficients are integral, so all resulting rational coefficients are integral and the binomial identity supplies the eighth power.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A_n=\sum_{k=0}^n \binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}^2
\]
be the Apéry number sequence A005259, and let
\[
a_n=\det(A_{i+j})_{0\leq i,j\leq n}.
\]
We prove that
\[
F(x):=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{a_n}{3^n}x^n
\]
is the eighth power of a power series in \(\mathbb Z[[x]]\). (If one defines the sequence using the absolute value of the determinant, as in the accepted formal setup, the determinants in question are nonnegative; in any event, every divisibility and power-series argument below works unchanged for signed determinants.)

We begin with congruences for the Apéry numbers.

### 1. The congruence \(A_n\equiv 1\pmod 4\)

We use the binomial identity
\[
\binom nk\binom{n+k}{k}
 =\binom{n+k}{2k}\binom{2k}{k}. \tag{1}
\]
For \(k\leq n\), this follows immediately by writing both sides in factorial form; for \(k>n\), both sides are zero. Also, for every \(k\geq 1\), the central binomial coefficient \(\binom{2k}{k}\) is even. One elementary proof is to write \(k=m+1\) and use Pascal's identity and symmetry:
\[
\binom{2m+2}{m+1}
 =\binom{2m+1}{m}+\binom{2m+1}{m+1}
 =2\binom{2m+1}{m}.
\]
Consequently, for \(k\geq1\), (1) shows that
\[
\binom nk^2\binom{n+k}{k}^2
 =\left(\binom nk\binom{n+k}{k}\right)^2
\]
is divisible by \(4\). The \(k=0\) summand is \(1\). Hence
\[
A_n\equiv1\pmod4 \qquad(n\geq0). \tag{2}
\]

### 2. The congruence \(A_n\equiv(-1)^n\pmod3\)

We first establish a base-three recurrence. Lucas's congruence in one digit says
\[
\binom nk\equiv
\binom{n\bmod3}{k\bmod3}\binom{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}{\lfloor k/3\rfloor}
\pmod3. \tag{3}
\]
Write \(n=3a+r\), where \(0\leq r<3\), and write a summation index as \(k=3b+s\), where \(0\leq s<3\). Applying (3) to the first binomial coefficient gives
\[
\binom{3a+r}{3b+s}\equiv \binom rs\binom ab\pmod3. \tag{4}
\]
For the second binomial coefficient, if \(r+s<3\), Lucas's congruence gives
\[
\binom{3a+r+3b+s}{3b+s}
 \equiv \binom{r+s}{s}\binom{a+b}{b}\pmod3. \tag{5}
\]
If \(r+s\geq3\), the same desired factorization of the complete summand remains true modulo \(3\), with both sides zero. Indeed, the low base-three digit on the left of (5) is \(r+s-3<s\), so the Lucas low-digit factor vanishes. On the right, the only possible pairs with \(r,s<3\) and \(r+s\geq3\) are \((1,2),(2,1),(2,2)\), and the corresponding coefficients \(\binom{r+s}{s}\) are \(3,3,6\), all divisible by \(3\).

After squaring (4) and the corresponding statement for the second factor, we therefore obtain, in every case,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\binom{3a+r}{3b+s}^{\!2}
 \binom{3a+r+3b+s}{3b+s}^{\!2}\\
&\qquad\equiv
\left(\binom rs^2\binom{r+s}{s}^2\right)
\left(\binom ab^2\binom{a+b}{b}^2\right)
\pmod3. \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]

In the sum defining \(A_{3a+r}\), we may extend the index range up to \(3(a+1)-1\), because all newly introduced terms have \(k>3a+r\) and hence \(\binom{3a+r}{k}=0\). Every index in that extended range is uniquely \(3b+s\), with \(0\leq b\leq a\) and \(0\leq s<3\). Thus (6) lets the sum factor modulo \(3\):
\[
A_{3a+r}\equiv
\left(\sum_{s=0}^2\binom rs^2\binom{r+s}{s}^2\right)A_a\pmod3. \tag{7}
\]
The short sum in parentheses is easily evaluated for the three possible values of \(r\). For \(r=0\) it is \(1\). For \(r=1\), its nonzero terms are \(1\) and \(4\), whose sum is \(5\equiv-1\pmod3\). For \(r=2\), the three terms are \(1,36,36\), whose sum is \(1\pmod3\). Hence
\[
A_{3a+r}\equiv(-1)^r A_a\pmod3. \tag{8}
\]

We now prove by strong induction that
\[
A_n\equiv(-1)^n\pmod3. \tag{9}
\]
The assertion is immediate for \(n=0\). If \(n=3a+r>0\), then \(a<n\), so (8) and the induction hypothesis give
\[
A_n\equiv(-1)^r(-1)^a=(-1)^{a+r}.
\]
Since \((3a+r)-(a+r)=2a\) is even, \((-1)^{a+r}=(-1)^{3a+r}=(-1)^n\), proving (9).

### 3. Divisibility of the Hankel determinants

We use the following elementary determinant observation. Let \(M\) be an \((N+1)\times(N+1)\) integer matrix. Suppose that, for each column \(j\geq1\), there is an integer \(\varepsilon_j\) such that
\[
M_{ij}\equiv \varepsilon_jM_{i0}\pmod p
\quad\text{for every row }i.
\]
Replace column \(j\) by column \(j-\varepsilon_j\) times column \(0\). These column operations leave the determinant unchanged. Every entry of each of the resulting \(N\) noninitial columns is divisible by \(p\), so one can factor \(p\) from each of those columns. Therefore
\[
p^N\mid\det M. \tag{10}
\]

Apply this to the Hankel matrix \(H_n=(A_{i+j})_{0\leq i,j\leq n}\). By (9),
\[
A_{i+j}\equiv(-1)^{i+j}=(-1)^j(-1)^i
              \equiv(-1)^j A_i\pmod3.
\]
Thus column \(j\) is congruent to \((-1)^j\) times column \(0\) modulo \(3\). Formula (10) gives
\[
3^n\mid a_n. \tag{11}
\]
Similarly, (2) implies
\[
A_{i+j}\equiv1\equiv A_i\pmod4,
\]
so every column is congruent to column \(0\) modulo \(4\), and (10) gives
\[
4^n\mid a_n. \tag{12}
\]

We will need a factor \(16\) in every nonconstant coefficient. For \(n\geq2\), this follows from \(4^n\mid a_n\). For \(n=1\), direct evaluation gives
\[
A_0=1,\qquad A_1=5,\qquad A_2=73,
\]
and hence
\[
a_1=\det\begin{pmatrix}1&5\\5&73\end{pmatrix}=73-25=48,
\]
which is also divisible by \(16\). Thus
\[
16\mid a_n\qquad(n\geq1). \tag{13}
\]
Also \(a_0=A_0=1\), so \(F(0)=1\).

### 4. The rational formal eighth root

Put
\[
w(x)=\sum_{n\geq1}a_nx^n\in\mathbb Z[[x]],
\qquad
u(x)=F(x)-1=\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{a_n}{3^n}x^n.
\]
By (11), \(a_n/3^n\) is an integer, although we will retain the displayed rational form because it records the divisibility needed below.

Since \(u(0)=0\), the formal binomial series can be substituted into \(u\). Define over \(\mathbb Q[[x]]\)
\[
C(x)=\sum_{d\geq0}\binom{1/8}{d}u(x)^d, \tag{14}
\]
where
\[
\binom{1/8}{d}
=\frac{(1/8)(1/8-1)\cdots(1/8-d+1)}{d!}.
\]
For any fixed coefficient of \(x^m\), only \(d\leq m\) contributes, so (14) is a well-defined formal power series. The formal binomial identity gives
\[
\left(\sum_{d\geq0}\binom{1/8}{d}X^d\right)^8=1+X.
\]
Substituting \(X=u(x)\), which is legitimate because \(u\) has zero constant term, yields
\[
C(x)^8=1+u(x)=F(x). \tag{15}
\]
It remains to prove the substantive point: every coefficient of \(C(x)\) is an integer.

For \(m,d\geq0\), let
\[
c_{m,d}=[x^m]w(x)^d\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Because \(u(x)=w(x/3)\), homogeneity of each degree gives
\[
[x^m]u(x)^d=3^{-m}c_{m,d}. \tag{16}
\]
The two determinant divisibilities give two corresponding divisibilities of \(c_{m,d}\). First, (11) lets us write
\[
w(x)=w_3(3x)
\]
for some \(w_3(x)\in\mathbb Z[[x]]\). Therefore the coefficient of degree \(m\) in \(w(x)^d=w_3(3x)^d\) is divisible by \(3^m\):
\[
3^m\mid c_{m,d}. \tag{17}
\]
Second, (13) gives \(w(x)=16v(x)\) for some \(v(x)\in\mathbb Z[[x]]\), and hence
\[
16^d\mid c_{m,d}. \tag{18}
\]
Finally, since \(w(0)=0\), we have \(c_{m,d}=0\) whenever \(d>m\), in agreement with the finiteness assertion above.

By (14) and (16),
\[
[x^m]C(x)=
\sum_{d=0}^m \binom{1/8}{d}3^{-m}c_{m,d}. \tag{19}
\]
We show that every summand in (19) is integral at every prime.

For a prime \(p\), write \(|\cdot|_p\) for the usual \(p\)-adic norm, normalized by \(|p|_p=p^{-1}\). We need two bounds for the generalized binomial coefficient.

First, if \(p\) is odd, then \(1/8\) is a \(p\)-adic integer, and
\[
\left|\binom{1/8}{d}\right|_p\leq1. \tag{20}
\]
For completeness, this is the standard integrality property of binomial polynomials on \(\mathbb Z_p\). It can be seen by approximating any \(z\in\mathbb Z_p\) by nonnegative integers \(n_j\). For fixed \(d\), the polynomial \(z\mapsto z(z-1)\cdots(z-d+1)/d!\) is continuous over \(\mathbb Q_p\); each \(\binom{n_j}{d}\) is an ordinary integer and therefore lies in the closed \(p\)-adic unit ball. Its limit \(\binom zd\) lies in that same closed ball. Taking \(z=1/8\) proves (20).

At \(p=2\), a precise weaker estimate suffices. From
\[
d!\binom{1/8}{d}=\prod_{i=0}^{d-1}(1/8-i)

after taking \(2\)-adic norms, observe that
\[
1/8-i=\frac{1-8i}{8},
\]
and \(1-8i\) is odd. Thus every factor on the right has \(2\)-adic norm \(8\), and the product has norm \(8^d\). Moreover, the exponent of \(2\) in \(d!\) is at most \(d\), so
\[
|d!|_2\geq2^{-d}.
\]
It follows that
\[
\left|\binom{1/8}{d}\right|_2
=\frac{8^d}{|d!|_2}
\leq 8^d2^d=16^d. \tag{21}
\]

Now fix a summand
\[
t_{m,d}=\binom{1/8}{d}3^{-m}c_{m,d}
\]
of (19).

If \(p=3\), (20) gives \(|\binom{1/8}{d}|_3\leq1\), while \(|3^{-m}|_3=3^m\). From (17),
\[
|c_{m,d}|_3\leq3^{-m}.
\]
Therefore
\[
|t_{m,d}|_3\leq1\cdot3^m\cdot3^{-m}=1. \tag{22}
\]

If \(p=2\), then \(|3^{-m}|_2=1\). By (18),
\[
|c_{m,d}|_2\leq |16^d|_2=16^{-d},
\]
and (21) gives
\[
|t_{m,d}|_2\leq16^d\cdot1\cdot16^{-d}=1. \tag{23}
\]

Finally, if \(p\neq2,3\), then (20) gives a bound of \(1\) for the binomial coefficient, \(|3^{-m}|_p=1\), and the integer \(c_{m,d}\) has norm at most \(1\). Hence again
\[
|t_{m,d}|_p\leq1. \tag{24}
\]

The nonarchimedean triangle inequality applied to the finite sum (19) now shows that
\[
|[x^m]C(x)|_p\leq1
\]
for every prime \(p\).

A rational number whose \(p\)-adic norm is at most \(1\) for every prime \(p\) is an integer. Indeed, write it in lowest terms as \(r/s\), with \(s>0\). If \(s>1\), choose a prime \(p\mid s\). Since the fraction is reduced, \(p\nmid r\), so its \(p\)-adic valuation is negative and its \(p\)-adic norm is greater than \(1\), a contradiction. Thus \(s=1\).

Applying this observation to every coefficient of \(C(x)\), we conclude that
\[
C(x)\in\mathbb Z[[x]].
\]
Together with (15), this proves
\[
\boxed{\;C(x)^8=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{a_n}{3^n}x^n\;}
\]
for an integer-coefficient power series \(C(x)\). Equivalently, \(\left(\sum_{n\geq0}a_nx^n/3^n\right)^{1/8}\) has integer coefficients, as claimed.
